analysis.body: {"transcript": {"text": "Number 9, Charles F. Barr et al. Petitioners v. City of Columbia. Mr. Perry, you may proceed with your argument. Mr. Chief Justice, may it please the court, this case is here on writ of certiorari to the Supreme Court of the State of South Carolina. Now, the case arose in March 1960, at which time the sit-in movement, or the movement which brings these cases before the court at this time, was perhaps at its highest stage. One day before this case arose, some of the petitioners in this case went to the office of the city manager of the City of Columbia to discuss matters pertaining to the efforts of Negroes to use lunch counter facilities in the City of Columbia. And at that conference, the record shows that the city manager of the City of Columbia advised some of these petitioners, gentlemen, further demonstrations will not be tolerated. At that particular time, most of the stores, drug stores, and other stores which had lunch counters in the City of Columbia, followed the policy of excluding Negroes or of segregating them therein. A few days before March 15, 1960, police officers working for the City of Columbia and other officers of the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division, working in cooperation with the City of Columbia, working in cooperation with the City of Columbia, learned that Negroes would make an effort to gain food service at the Taylor Street Pharmacy located in the City of Columbia. Agent Carl Stokes of the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division testified that he and other officers advised the management of Taylor Street Pharmacy that Negroes were coming. They had some meeting among themselves and worked out a plan whereby the action which was thereafter taken was formulated. This plan was that, among other things, that officers would be placed in the premises of the Taylor Street Pharmacy. On March 15, 1960, Agent Carl Stokes of the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division and a deputy sheriff were on duty in the Taylor Street Pharmacy premises. They'd been waiting there throughout the morning, up until the time the five petitioners here appeared. When the petitioners entered the store, they walked in quietly and some of them stopped near the front of the store to purchase some cards. The Solicitor General's argument was that the Solicitor General was going to be moved and a time to take the three minutes to work and serve. Well, they might have known it, Mr. Justice Goldberg. The Solicitor General's argument on the vagueness of the statute here might still have merit because, of course, the statute did not give these petitioners any warning. They may have known, but this statute didn't. They were told this officially by the city manager of the city of Columbia. However, petitioner David Carter testified at the trial that he did not know he would not be served and that, in fact, he went there to be served. I would say that he was expressing some optimism, sir. After some of the petitioners stopped to buy postcards or other cards, they then started walking to the rear of the store. Now, here, perhaps I should state the layout of the store. The Taylor Street Pharmacy is a very large drugstore in the city of Columbia. In fact, it is described by its manager as a department store. It also has a restaurant which is located near the rear or at the rear of the store premises. The petitioners started walking back there, and Agent Carl Stokes, together with the deputy sheriff, followed them in close pursuit because this was the kind of thing that Agent Stokes and the deputy sheriff were waiting for. And as the petitioners went into the restaurant area, some of them, all of them, took seats at different points. The manager of the store came into the lunchroom area and stationed himself at a point where he thought his voice could be heard by all, and stated that the Negroes would not be served and that they would have to leave. At this time, Agent Stokes was standing right by the manager, there in close proximity to him. And after the store manager had made his statement and the petitioners did not move, Agent Stokes leaned over and said to the manager, Now you go over and tell each one of them in person or directly to leave in my presence. Acting in response to the request of the police officer, Mr. Terry, the manager, went over to each of the petitioners, all except one of them, and told them that they would have to leave. That is, with Agent Stokes still following in close pursuit. Agent Stokes was a policeman? Yes, sir. Agent Stokes was an officer of the South Carolina Law Enforcement Division. After... Does that mean the state police? That's a long word. That is correct, sir. The South Carolina Law Enforcement Division is the official police force of the state of South Carolina. We ran into that, I think, in the Edwards. That is correct, in Edwards versus South Carolina. After the manager had directed the Negroes to leave, he then left the area of the lunch counter, or of the restaurant. One of the petitioners sought to have some words with him on the way out, but the manager said, I have nothing further to say, and kept leaving the place. At this point, then, Agent Stokes and the deputy sheriff took over completely, with petitioners still occupying their seats, in the same manner which had characterized their conduct before the manager left. And at this point, Mr. Stokes, the SLED agent, stated to the petitioners, now I am a state officer, and I am saying to you, you will have to leave. At this point, assuming you're putting aside your constitutional arguments, at this point an offense had been committed, had it not? I am saying to you, but I am saying to you, that the law enforcement officers take over, because an offense had been committed under the state law. Well, in our view, no offense at that time had been committed, because the petitioners had done nothing... ...except stay there after they'd been told to leave. That is correct. And the only reason for the request which was made to them to leave was because they're Negroes. Well, as I say, putting to one side the constitutional argument, as a matter of state law, an offense had been then committed, after they'd stayed there, after being told to leave, had it not? An offense which has been defined by South Carolina to constitute an offense. Exactly. Yes, sir. That is correct, Mr. Justice Goldberg. We did, however, contend that the petitioners were pursuing their constitutional right of freedom of speech and of oppression. Yes, sir. You take the point to the constitutional argument. That is correct. It was not specifically raised at the trial, except to the extent that it might have been raised in the contention that petitioners were exercising rights of freedom of speech. So was it argued in any state of the state? Not specifically. Not specifically. When Agent Stokes said to the petitioners, all right now, I'm a police officer and you'll have to leave. The petitioners kept their seats. The petitioners kept their seats. He thereupon placed them under arrest and told them to follow me, at which time all of the petitioners followed Agent Stokes out of the store and got into his police car. Now, these petitioners were thereupon charged in warrants issued by the City of Columbia with trespass under Section 16386 of the South Carolina Code of Laws for 1952 at that time. And I might say, parenthetically, that since that time, South Carolina has recodified under the 1962 code and the 19, the section to which we refer as Section 16386 under the 1952 code is now codified by the same numerical number in the 1962 code. So is it just from what the court is made or what the court is made? There is no change made. It's copied verbatim. So the corporate change is protected. That is correct. However, shortly after these cases reached the court in March 1960, South Carolina enacted a new statute, which was before this court last year, in Peterson v. City of Greenville, now codified as Section 16-388. Petitioners were also charged with breach of peace under a statute which is set forth in the record of these proceedings as Section 16509. Where do you find that statute? The court is set forth in Petitioner's Brief at page 3. I beg your pardon. I have misstated the numerical section. Section 15909. This is the first time that particular statute had been invoked. The court will recall that we were here in Edwards v. South Carolina, at which time the court convicted petitioners of the common law offense of breach of peace. But throughout these proceedings, the convictions of petitioners here have been referred to as violations of the particular section to which we refer. Petitioners were tried in the municipal court of the city of Columbia, known as the recorders court, and were found guilty of the crimes of trespass and of breach of peace. The Ritzland County Court affirmed, as did the South Carolina Supreme Court later, rejecting petitioners' claims that their constitutional rights had been violated, and rejecting further petitioners' claim that the evidence presented against them did not support the charge made on the ground that the exceptions which petitioners made were said to have been too general. However, this was the first time in this series of cases that the court had invoked such a rule. And in fact, in other cases decided about the same time, ruled upon exceptions identical to those which were framed in this case. The convictions under both statutes were affirmed? Were they, Mr. Perry? Both. Yes, sir. That is correct. And breach of peace? And breach of peace. Or disorderly conduct? That is correct. That is correct. The statute is entitled disorderly conduct. Disorderly conduct. But it includes a multitude of offenses. It does, yes. Including breach of peace. And all of these petitioners were convicted under both? That is correct. And convictions under both were affirmed? Were affirmed, yes, sir. And were concurrent or consecutive sentences imposed? Or consecutive sentences were imposed in these cases, with $24.50 of each sentence being suspended. We do not know what brought about the particular formula the court used, except that it represented some arbitrary concept on the part of the court. And the police, in this case, in this case, was a very clear-cut illustration of the use of state power to enforce racial segregation. The police, in this case, came into the matter before petitioners ever went upon the premises of Taylor Street Pharmacy. They warned the manager, in fact, that Negroes were coming. And the white saw the role of Paul Revere, the redcoats are coming. Yes, sir. That's all the records show. It's just that Negroes are coming. That is correct. And they also counseled the manager in the method in which the criminal offense was to be charged and the evidence secured in order to later go to court and prosecute. Because... I missed that. All right, sir. Agent Carl Stokes testified that he stood next to the manager and after the manager told the petitioners, I will not serve you, you will have to leave, the agent, carrying the full palomptu of South Carolina power, stood next to the manager and said to him, Now you go and tell each one of these petitioners, each one of these persons, he will have to leave. In my presence. In my presence. Stokes was this so-called sled man. That is correct. And the deputy sheriff also was on the premises and standing close by. Did he say anything to the manager? The record does not show that the deputy sheriff said anything. I believe that respect and deference was given to the agent from the official police force of the state of South Carolina. I think Agent Stokes outranked the deputy sheriff. And the record indicates that he did most of the active cooperation with the management in this case. The record also shows that he counseled with him before the Negroes came, while the Negroes were upon the premises, and in fact arrested the petitioners without having been requested to do so by the manager. The record is significant. The record is significant. Well, I think that it is significant for the purpose of illustrating to this court the extent to which the power of the state was used as a matter of state law. Well, I think what happened here, remembering my brother Goldberg's question in the previous case as to whether or not it's the duty of a police officer to arrest somebody simply because he's requested to do so. And the answer is obviously no in any state. But certainly the other side of the coin is that it is the duty of a police officer to arrest somebody if a misdemeanor is committed in his presence, regardless of whether or not he's requested to do so. Isn't that true? Well, while that may be true, sir, I submit to the court that whereas here the state had no statute specifically prohibiting this conduct, the city of Columbia had no ordinance specifically prohibiting it, as was the case in Peterson v. Greenville, the state officer requested and demanded that petitioners leave. He thereby made it a crime for them to thereafter remain. And when they refused to immediately leave, the power of the state further went into operation by carrying forth an arrest, which was not requested by the manager. And we submit that this is important for the purpose of illustrating the extent of the full power of use by the police. What you're saying in effect is that this record shows that the state is there not to enforce property rights but to enforce segregation. That's precisely our position. Now, implicit at least in these records and these cases come up in a very skimpy way, you have none. Implicit in this, wouldn't you think it was fair to say that there's a, the state court at least, rightly or wrongly thought, in the contrary. In other words, it recognized that the state could not do what you're claiming it did. The state court recognized a right on the part of management to exclude Negroes and thereby declared a state law policy, which we feel violates petitioners' rights to both equal protection and impotence. Well, a little off, at least what I was trying to say, you're making a specific statement that because of the advance notice of this, of the police, of Stokes, he was, Stokes, that Negroes are coming to the restaurant, and his action on the premises in arresting without waiting, without the request of the owner, and other things that you said, all add up to something that indicates that the state was really enforcing segregation here rather than enforcing the trespass law. Yes, sir, precisely. Precisely. And I think that when we examine that against the background of statutes in South Carolina, which specifically require racial segregation, and the custom which these statutes seem to have generated. Yes, but you're getting off again on a broader subject. I'm dealing with a particular thing because, as far as I'm concerned, if you can demonstrate what you show, you're entitled to a reversal of this case. But I can't see it in the record yet. That's what I'm... Well, sir, I think that it's in the record right from the beginning of the first warning that Agent Stokes and other officers conveyed to the manager that Negroes were coming. I think it's also apparent in the record when Agent Stokes and the deputy sheriff went on duty on the store premises. I think it is also apparent that when petitioners were entering the restaurant, Agent Stokes and the deputy sheriff followed them in close pursuit, this being their primary purpose on the premises. I think it is... Is there a little ambiguity in the record? It's clear that there have been an advance agreement between the police and the rest of the world against what must be done. The ambiguity I found in the record is this. It's fake. It's not clear on the record that the police said, the authorities said to the member of the rest of the house. In order for us to execute a policy of discrimination, you've got a request. It is clear to what you said in this testimony that Mr. Stokes was advising the opponent of the manager. The police said, the commissioners came from the police or came from the store now? That's what happened. I don't know that I'm going to get it. I think, Mr. Justice Goldberg, if you will go back to the first one or two statements I made, which appears in the testimony of a petition of David Carter, prior to the entry into the Taylor Street drugstore premises, these young men had been in to see the city manager, and he had said to them, gentlemen, further demonstrations will not be tolerated. I believe we have to begin there to see exactly where the statement on the part of the police of the city of Columbia came from and where the full power of the government of South Carolina came from.
